source.title: Same Concept, Different Directions: Cross-Modal Feature Heterogeneity in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Chung-Pa Lee; Jihoon Kwon; Kyle Min; Jy-yong Sohn

record.tranche_reason: The study examines cross-modal feature-direction mismatch and modality split, not whether increasing an SAE dictionary size splits a feature into finer features that partition its inputs. Its results concern a related but distinct phenomenon.
record.gate_note: The paper reports measurements of cross-modal feature directions and synthetic cross-modal feature collapse, recorded below as findings about a related construct. It does not sweep dictionary size or test whether finer features partition a smaller feature's inputs. Results comparing the proposed retrieval and alignment method with other methods are not included because they do not measure the claim's feature-splitting behavior.
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-modal feature heterogeneity (image vs text decoder directions for the same concept) and modality split in multimodal SAEs. It never varies dictionary size to see whether coarse features split into finer ones. It does not test absorption, hierarchy, canonical units, or Matryoshka objectives. Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 concern capacity (m < 2n vs m ≥ 2n) collapsing or separating cross-modal directions. That bears on a different construct: one concept in two modalities, not one feature splitting into finer subfeatures. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the same concept has different image and text feature directions, and that this drives modality split in shared SAEs. Auxiliary alignment losses trade reconstruction for alignment. Modality-specific SAEs with post-hoc Hungarian alignment preserve reconstruction and improve retrieval and steering.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures cross-modal feature-direction heterogeneity and modality split, and compares shared with modality-specific SAEs; it does not train SAEs at increasing dictionary sizes or measure within-modality feature partitions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports cross-modal heterogeneity for base- and large-size VLMs. In its separate downstream evaluation, retrieval performance varies with Top-K sparsity level, backbone, and sparsifying activation function.

fits_no_version.finding: In four base and four large VLMs, highly coactivated image-text SAE feature pairs do not concentrate near zero cosine distance. The two examples have distances 0.42 and 0.50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantically corresponding image and text features in VLM joint embeddings occupy distinct directions (cross-modal feature heterogeneity).

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic data, a shared SAE collapses close but distinct cross-modal directions, with higher reconstruction and feature-recovery error. Parameter-matched modality-specific SAEs avoid this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The SAE reconstruction objective separates or collapses cross-modal directions depending on geometry and capacity, producing modality split.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: Semantic correspondence is inferred from coactivation correlation rather than known labels in the real-embedding analysis. The cross-modal distance distributions and synthetic curves are presented as figures without exact values in the text. The theory uses the linear representation hypothesis and simplified generative assumptions; the authors note that coactivation-based correspondence may be less accurate in noisy or weakly aligned settings.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep, no coarse-to-fine partition of inputs, no split-feature direction comparison.
Larger VLMs are analysed only for cross-modal direction mismatch, not for size-driven splitting or across open SAE releases.
No nested feature families or concept hierarchy.
No parent/child latent firing or absorption measurement.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes.
No test that splitting arises from the sparsity objective on hierarchical inputs; no Matryoshka comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The record's links to 'none' and its T6 / discusses classification are appropriate. The rows are correctly scoped to a related construct. Method-comparison results (Tables 1–4, Figures 6–8) are rightly excluded. There is a loose analogy to V6 (the objective decides whether directions split or merge), but it concerns cross-modal pairs, not size-driven splitting, so it is not a test of V6.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size comparison, within-modality feature splitting, input partition test, or comparison of split-feature directions.
The study tests cross-modal feature heterogeneity across several VLMs, not whether the dictionary-size splitting pattern holds at scale or across SAE families or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families or concept hierarchy are tested.
No parent-child latent firing or absorption behavior is tested.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, or addition of novel latents across dictionary sizes, is tested.
The paper does not test whether size-related feature splitting is caused by the sparsity objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or compare Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine distances between image and text SAE decoder features, grouped by paired-latent coactivation correlation.
rows.measure: Distribution of cosine distances between estimated image-text feature directions
rows.baseline: Perfect directional alignment would give cosine distance near 0
rows.value: The distribution remains centered around a positive value and does not concentrate near zero, including for high-correlation pairs; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The paper treats coactivation correlation as a proxy for semantic correspondence; the result is cross-modal direction mismatch, not dictionary-size splitting.

rows.subject: Shared SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured whether same-concept image and text features are assigned to one learned direction.

conditions.value: varied; nonzero distances, including geometrically close but distinct directions

rows.baseline: Modality-specific SAEs avoid merging the two modality-specific directions
rows.value: The shared SAE exhibits feature collapse when the image and text directions are geometrically close but not identical; exact rates are figure-only.
rows.note: This is cross-modal collapse under a shared SAE, not splitting of one feature across increasing dictionary sizes.

rows.subject: Modality-specific SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Measured whether same-concept image and text features are assigned to one learned direction.

conditions.value: varied; nonzero distances, including geometrically close but distinct directions

rows.baseline: Shared SAE collapses some geometrically close but nonidentical cross-modal feature directions
rows.value: Separate modality-specific SAEs avoid this collapse; exact rates are figure-only.
rows.note: This is a comparison of cross-modal feature recovery arrangements, not a dictionary-size splitting test.

relation.reason: Fits. Theorem 1 discusses how limited latent capacity merges close directions into one latent, but the paper does not test splitting.

tranche.reason: The study measures cross-modal feature heterogeneity and modality split. It never varies dictionary size and never mentions feature splitting, absorption or Matryoshka SAEs.

source_check.notes: Rows r1, r2, r11 and r12 match the text. Values are figure-only. r1 and r2 use modality-specific SAEs (m=8192, K=8). The Fig 3 examples (CLIP ViT-B/32) have c=0.67 and 0.63, below the c>=0.8 bin. Theorem 1 (m<2n vs m>=2n) is a stylized capacity argument next to splitting, not a dictionary-size test.

statements.problem: None. Four base VLMs (Fig 2) and four large VLMs (Fig 9, App. E.1) are both reported. The paper itself calls the 0.42 and 0.50 examples high-coactivation pairs. The synthetic result and the parameter matching are as stated.
